item.title: All of a Sudden, 2026 - ★★★★★
item.description: Loved this. very consistent. The date cards are probably the most legible thing in the film and the easiest to ignore. A day, then another, passed. Everything else in it ask or insinuated what time is for(?); the caregivers complain that the methods cost them hours and also of course, the main thesis—the suddenness of mortality—all of this urgent themes laid upon early in the film, and yet Hamaguchi intentionally insist to spends most of his runtime with restraint. Conversations played out until they run dry, really exercising humanitude as the methods one of the character implies; as how giving someone your time to care, and the film also does it to it's character and to the audience. When it ended, thus, it felt peaceful, in some sense.

item.title: La Bola Negra, 2026 - ★★★★
item.description:
the melodrama really swells here, and it's also gorgeous, it just lets the feeling be bigger than the scene. they really get this part right. loved me myself some maximalist movies.

but then, my quarrel is with some of the war shoot. The dead are composed like still life, couldnt stop debating over myself whether this is an ethic of the image or just an aesthetic of alibi? what it cost to make the intolerable vieweable (or consumable). here the answer seems to be that the cost is the intolerable itself. looks like beauty lauders the horror. it trying to have both an authority as historical witness, and yet also wanting the pleasure of tableau and refuses to choose which weights more.

the timelines also run in parallel yet never truly contamined one another. which i dont really have problem with, but it does made me wonder what couldve been if they treated this one like Sound of Falling, with the visual consistency across generation.

so yeah. undeniably it's very well made, well shot, well acted, but it's a lot. the ambition is huge, and as spectacle it lands just fine. what i'm less sure about is the creative judgement. i don't think it quite gets some of its choices right.

item.title: Tell Everyone, 2026 - ★★★★½
item.description:
oh my. i did not see this coming, and i liked it more than the melodrama i just watched, which is a sentence i'm still a little surprised to be typing, lol.

the thing is it offers so little, but it just executed flawlessly. there are no experiments with narrative flow, no gambling on formal choices, the screenplay is very straight and somehow that's probably the point? there's a kind of rigor in refusing to perform. the film trusts the scene and it's character, and doesn't reach past what it needs.

what i keep circling back to tho is the gaze. it's inoffensive in the best sense, i mean ethically inoffensive: it never once turns exploitative, not even when it has to look at a tragedy. there's a whole old argument about where the camera goes being a moral question, and here you just won't really find any problem with the shots. except, there's one shot maybe. Where i did wonder about the intention, whether it was needed. but again, theres only one shot over the whole movies that popped up a question in my mind, i take that as a win.

very good. genuinely did not expect it to be this good.

item.title: 2024 End Year List: Documentary
item.description:
This year, I decided to separate fiction and documentary films in my end-of-year list. So much has happened in the world, and just ranking them as personal favorites felt wrong—it seemed to downplay the urgency of the issues we’re facing.

  • No Other Land

    There is no other documentary you need to watch more than this one. Against the backdrop of the ongoing Gaza genocide, No Other Land offers a searing portrayal of perpetual colonialism and the brutal realities faced by Palestinian villagers in Masafer Yatta. The film’s raw, unflinching narrative exposes the structural violence and relentless demolitions inflicted upon these communities while celebrating their unyielding spirit of resistance.

  • Soundtrack to a Coup d'Etat

    Through archival footage and an chaoting editing, Grimonprez navigates this complex episode of the start of Pax Americana order. His approach to storytelling mirrors the improvisational nature of jazz, where rhythms of tension and release echo the political upheavals of the time. Despite the intensity and fragmented nature of the visuals, Grimonprez ensures that the documentary never loses sight of its central message. The chaotic flow of images, sounds, and voices comes together in a way that distills the heart of this historical moment, making it comprehensible even to those unfamiliar with cold-war international politics.

  • Monisme

    I liked the post-colonial approach in Monisme, remind me much of Weerasethakul's Memoria (2021). What struck me most was how Rizaldi uses the figure of the mystic as a counter-narrative to the modern, scientific, rational Western worldview. Rizaldi doesn’t present this indigenous worldview in opposition to the scientist’s rationalism in a simplistic, binary way. Instead, both perspectives coexist within the film’s polyphonic structure, each presenting a legitimate form of knowledge, without privileging one over the other.

  • Dahomey

    As I wrote this excerpt, i realize the movies on my list are underlined an ongoing relevance of the post-colonial movement and its exploration of the lasting effects of colonialism. Each film, in its unique way, speaks to the complexities of power, identity, and on this, restitution,

    On Dahomey, Mati Diop brings a poetic sensibility to this weighty topic, elevating the narrative beyond legal or political debates into something far more human and profound. The objects being returned represent the stories, identities, and legacies of a people who were once colonized and stripped of their history.

  • The Gullspång Miracle

    Encapsulating the notion that life is stranger than fiction, it employs layered narratives that juggle the complexities of identity construction. Each twist and piece of information could becomes its own intriguing story. Maria Fredriksson’s direction has this uncanny ability to pull you into the mystery, and by the end, I couldn’t stop thinking about how fragile our understanding of “truth” really is. This is the kind of documentary that lingers in my mind long after the credits roll.

    Human stories, as this illustrates, can be both fascinating and terrifying.
